items.definition: able to continue over time without causing harm

examples.source: During the discussion, the habit seemed sustainable once everyone had examined the evidence carefully.
examples.translation: Während des Gesprächs wirkte die Gewohnheit dauerhaft tragfähig, nachdem alle die Belege sorgfältig geprüft hatten.

examples.source: Although the habit appeared sustainable at first, the wider context revealed several practical possibilities.
examples.translation: Obwohl die Gewohnheit zunächst dauerhaft tragfähig erschien, zeigte der größere Zusammenhang mehrere praktische Möglichkeiten.

examples.source: Her account showed why a more sustainable habit could influence decisions long after the immediate moment.
examples.translation: Ihre Darstellung zeigte, warum eine stärker dauerhaft tragfähig geprägte Sicht auf die Gewohnheit Entscheidungen noch lange nach dem unmittelbaren Moment beeinflussen konnte.

items.definition: to continue following a regular pattern

examples.source: The group decided to stick to a routine before committing to a final course of action.
examples.translation: Die Gruppe beschloss, sich an eine Routine halten, bevor sie sich auf ein endgültiges Vorgehen festlegte.

examples.source: Experienced people know when to stick to a routine, especially when circumstances change unexpectedly.
examples.translation: Erfahrene Menschen wissen, wann sie sich an eine Routine halten sollten, besonders wenn sich die Umstände unerwartet ändern.

examples.source: By choosing to stick to a routine, they avoided a problem that might otherwise have become much harder to resolve.
examples.translation: Indem sie sich entschieden, sich an eine Routine halten, vermieden sie ein Problem, das sonst deutlich schwieriger zu lösen gewesen wäre.

pages.text: Leonie arrived at a workplace wellbeing programme that had previously relied on short-lived challenges. The setting felt sustainable, but the people involved did not yet share a clear plan. Rather than rushing towards an answer, Leonie asked the group to stick to a routine and explain what success would mean in practice.

A second difficulty soon emerged. The existing approach looked sedentary to some participants, while others feared that the change would create new problems. They agreed to prioritise wellbeing so that every perspective could be tested against the same evidence instead of personal preference.

The most restorative moment came when a quiet participant questioned the assumption behind the original plan. Leonie encouraged everyone to listen to your body. That pause did not weaken the discussion; it made the risks visible and allowed the group to respond with more care.

By the afternoon, one part of the proposal seemed resilient. The group therefore chose to break a habit rather than defend an option simply because time had already been invested in it. The decision created room for a practical alternative that nobody had considered that morning.

One final issue remained detrimental. To resolve it, the participants had to maintain a balance while keeping their shared purpose in view. Leonie summarised the strongest points, invited one last objection and made sure that the next steps had clear owners.

The result was a flexible routine that improved energy, sleep and trust across the team. Nobody pretended that uncertainty had disappeared, yet the group left with a decision they could explain and support. Leonie reflected that progress rarely comes from certainty alone; it comes from precise language, attentive listening and the courage to revise a plan.
